the evolutionary mechanism of natural selection. When antibiotics are used, they kill most bacteria, but some may possess genetic mutations that allow them to survive the treatment. These resistant bacteria then reproduce, passing on their resistance traits to their offspring. Over time, this leads to the emergence of antibiotic-resistant strains.

Overprescription of antibiotics accelerates this process. When antibiotics are used unnecessarily or inappropriately—such as for viral infections—they kill off susceptible bacteria, leaving behind those that are already resistant. This creates an environment where resistant strains can dominate and spread more easily. Additionally, the excessive and improper use of antibiotics in agriculture and livestock further contributes to the development and spread of resistance.

Examples of antibiotic-resistant bacteria include MRSA (Methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus*) and multidrug-resistant *Escherichia coli*. These strains pose significant challenges to public health because they are difficult to treat with conventional antibiotics.

Antibiotic resistance arises through the evolutionary mechanism of natural selection. When antibiotics are used, they kill most bacteria, but some may possess genetic mutations that allow them to survive the treatment. These resistant bacteria then reproduce, passing on their resistance traits to their offspring. Over time, this leads to the emergence of antibiotic-resistant strains.

Overprescription of antibiotics accelerates this process. When antibiotics are used unnecessarily or inappropriately—such as for viral infections—they kill off susceptible bacteria, leaving behind those that are already resistant. This creates an environment where resistant strains can dominate and spread more easily. Additionally, the excessive and improper use of antibiotics in agriculture and livestock further contributes to the development and spread of resistance.

Examples of antibiotic-resistant bacteria include MRSA (Methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus*) and multidrug-resistant *Escherichia coli*. These strains pose significant challenges to public health because they are difficult to treat with conventional antibiotics.
